title: Eviction spike: root cause hypothesis, signalization, and safeties
creator: Aditi Rao
description: Summary: On 2026-03-09 we observed a transient, high-frequency spike in batch eviction events on several inference hosts after a scheduler heuristic tweak rolled to 30% of traffic. Symptoms included an increase in p95/p99 token-latency, a small bump in 5xxs for affected models, and amplified GPU kernel churn leading to reduced throughput. This ticket captures the working hypothesis, immediate mitigations, follow-ups for observability, and long-term safeguards to prevent recurrence.
incident_timeline: 2026-03-09 02:10 UTC: Canary rollout of scheduler affinity damping (runtime-1.22) begins.
2026-03-09 02:23 UTC: Grafana alert: batch_evictions_per_min > 50 on pool-us-west-2a; oncall notified.
2026-03-09 02:27 UTC: Traffic diverted from canary to stable; eviction counts dropped but not to baseline.
2026-03-09 03:40 UTC: Temporary rollback of affinity damping completed; latency returned to baseline by 03:55 UTC.
2026-03-09 05:00 UTC: Incident declared; postmortem investigation started.
root_cause_hypothesis: A recent change to the scheduler's probe window and affinity damping reduced kernel residency time for warmed KV-cache entries, causing more frequent batch evictions under bursty arrival patterns.
Evictions triggered unbatched or under-populated kernel launches which increased per-token latency and increased load on the kernel selector, causing secondary oscillation.
A telemetry gap: we lacked fine-grained signals correlating eviction events to KV-cache hit rates and per-model probe counts, making fast triage difficult.
proposed_immediate_actions: Quarantine the scheduler heuristic change in the canary branch and stop further rollout (done 2026-03-09).
Patch: add an emergency circuit that prevents probe-window shrink below a conservative lower bound when eviction rate > X (implement X=40/min for test).
Roll out a short-term autoscaler guard: when eviction spike detected, throttle new allocation probing to avoid amplifying churn.
Add an alert that correlates eviction spikes with per-model KV-cache miss ratio and kernel-launch-counts.
Create a synthetic load reproduction in staging that reproduces bursty arrivals and validates fixes (owner: Marcus Li).
Open a canary verification run before re-rolling heuristic (owner: SRE team).
Add an automatic rollback plan to the deployment pipeline if p95 increases 20% above baseline during canary.
Add a short-term rate-limit on probing frequency for the first 30s of newly scheduled worker lifetime to allow KV-cache pre-warm.
Coordinate with Customer Success: identify customers affected and flag for follow-up if any SLA exposures.
longer_term_followups: Design and implement a kernel-eviction telemetry surface: per-kernel eviction reasons, per-model probe counts, per-worker KV-cache hit curves (owner: Observability).
Refactor scheduler probing so that probe decisions are informed by recent KV-cache hit history and batch fill ratios rather than purely timer-based heuristics.
Introduce a canary matrix that runs heuristics at low qps and gradually increases while measuring eviction and latency signals automatically.
Benchmark different probe-window tradeoffs across representative workloads and publish a recommended default profile per model family.
Hardening: implement a damping layer that prevents oscillatory probe ramp when multiple nodes experience eviction simultaneously.
Postmortem doc + playbook: add a dedicated runbook for eviction spikes with triage checklist, telemetry queries, and rollback thresholds.
acceptance_criteria: Staging reproduction: synthetic test reproduces eviction spike; patch mitigates spike without increasing baseline latency.
Telemetry: new eviction -> KV-cache hit correlation dashboard is live and has alerting configured.
Canary gating: deployment pipeline enforces automatic rollback on p95 degradation during canaries.
No recurrence on next 2 production canaries (monitored for 72h each).

notes_for_review: Decision trade-offs: we prefer a conservative probe lower bound for short-term safety at the cost of slightly slower model adaptation to load bursts. Long-term we should move to a metric-driven probe rather than fixed timers.
Risk: if the lower bound is too high, we may increase steady-state memory pressure; monitoring for GPU memory eviction regressions is required.
